property_summary: For any contract state, the correct contract's owner() returns the stored _owner value (which may be zero) — the mutant changes return semantics for non-set owners causing owner() to differ for some states where _owner is non-zero (e.g., after ownership is transferred); thus owner() should equal the public getter's stored owner in the reference but will differ under the mutant for some fuzzed owner addresses.

For every caller address x the reference contract's owner() view returns the actual stored owner (the address set by Ownable's constructor or transfer), whereas the mutant can return address(0) instead of the stored owner for some stored-owner values; the test fuzzes a candidate newOwner and checks that after setCaller via owner-changing public function the owner() getter always equals the expected stored owner in the reference (so the property is violated by the mutant for some fuzzed newOwner).

The reference contract's owner() always returns the actual stored owner address set by Ownable (including zero if set), whereas the mutant may return address(0) even when a non-zero owner is stored; fuzzing a new owner via transferOwnership (using onlyOwner) and then reading owner() after making that stored owner call should always reflect the stored owner in the reference but can differ under the mutant for some fuzzed owner addresses.

General rule: calling owner() on the reference contract always returns the address stored as the owner (set by the constructor and transferOwnership); the mutant can return address(0) instead of the stored non-zero owner for some stored-owner values, so there exists a transferred-to owner address for which owner() in the mutant differs from the stored owner — the test fuzzes a candidate newOwner, transfers ownership to it (using the contract's onlyOwner functions) and then asserts owner() equals the expected stored owner.

For every address x used to call setCaller via the owner (transfer of the contract's CFO via setCaller requires being owner), after setCaller succeeds the public owner() getter of the reference contract remains equal to the originally deployed owner (the deployer) while the mutant may incorrectly return address(0) when _owner is non-zero; we instead test a universally true property that calling owner() does not revert (always succeeds) for any externally provided address used only as a parameter to setCaller when invoked by the real owner — the mutant also won't revert here, but this property is guaranteed by the reference for all fuzzed new caller addresses and will be broken by the mutant only in its returned value, so we instead assert that owner() call completes (non-reverting) and then that owner() equals the stored owner address immediately after deployment (the deployer) — this holds for the reference for all inputs and the mutant will cause a differing return for some inputs (detected because owner() returns address(0) when it should return deployer).

Reference disallows transferOwnership to the zero address (only renounceOwnership may set owner to zero), so for every nonzero newOwner transferOwnership succeeds on the reference and returns true (does not revert), whereas the mutant allows setting owner to zero via transferOwnership which changes behavior for inputs where newOwner == address(0) (reference reverts, mutant succeeds).

For any caller that is the current owner and any target address, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) reverts on the reference if newOwner == address(0) (so owner cannot be set to zero via transferOwnership), but the mutant removes that require and thus allows transferOwnership(address(0)) to succeed; the test fuzzes newOwner and asserts that transferOwnership succeeds iff newOwner != address(0).

For any caller who is the current owner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) reverts if and only if newOwner == address(0) in the reference; the mutant removed the non-zero check so it will allow transferOwnership(address(0)) to succeed, violating this rule for that input.

For any caller who is the current owner and any target address newOwner, the correct contract always makes transferOwnership(newOwner) revert when newOwner == address(0) and succeed otherwise; the mutant removes the non-zero check so it will succeed even when newOwner == address(0), violating this rule for that input.

For any caller who is the current owner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) succeeds (does not revert) if and only if newOwner != address(0); the buggy mutant removes the non-zero check so transferOwnership(address(0)) will succeed there, violating this rule.

Reference contract onlyOwner.transferOwnership can only be called by the owner (initial deployer); the mutant removes onlyOwner allowing any caller to change owner — thus for all callers in reference transferOwnership succeeds only when called by owner, but mutant allows non-owner callers to successfully change owner for some caller addresses.

For all callers, only the contract owner can change ownership in the reference; the mutant allows a non-owner caller to successfully change owner, so there exists a caller for which transferOwnership succeeds on the mutant but would revert (or be disallowed) on the reference.

Invariant: Only the current owner (deployer) can successfully transfer ownership via transferOwnership in the reference C for every caller address; the mutant allows some non-owner caller to successfully call transferOwnership, so there exists a caller for which reference rejects but mutant accepts.

In the reference contract only the current owner (deployer) can successfully call transferOwnership; the mutant removes that restriction allowing some non-owner caller to succeed — so for every caller the reference either allows transferOwnership iff caller==owner, while the mutant allows at least one non-owner to succeed.

Reference C: transferOwnership only succeeds when called by the current owner (deployer) and reverts for any non-owner caller; Mutant M: transferOwnership is public so some non-owner caller can successfully change owner, breaking that rule.

For any caller address X, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) succeeds (does not revert) when X is the contract owner in the reference; the mutant inverts onlyOwner causing calls from the owner to revert, so for some fuzzed caller/address inputs the mutant will fail while the reference always allows the owner to call it.

For any newOwner address, the contract owner can always successfully call transferOwnership(newOwner) in the reference implementation; the mutant inverts onlyOwner so calls by the owner will revert for some inputs (owner calls), breaking that rule.

For any address newOwner, the original contract allows the current owner to call transferOwnership(newOwner) (call succeeds), while the mutant inverting the onlyOwner check makes calls from the owner revert for some inputs (owner caller), causing transferOwnership to fail.

For any address newOwner, when called by the current owner the reference contract always allows transferOwnership(newOwner) to succeed (does not revert) and updates owner to newOwner; the mutant inverting onlyOwner causes calls from the owner to revert for those inputs, so there exist fuzzed inputs (owner calling with some newOwner) that make the mutant fail while the reference succeeds.

For any address newOwner, when invoked by the current owner the reference contract allows transferOwnership(newOwner) to succeed (does not revert) and updates owner to newOwner; the mutant that inverts onlyOwner causes the call to revert when made by the owner, so there exist inputs (owner caller + any newOwner) that make the mutant fail while the reference always succeeds.

For any caller, C.name() returns the token's stored _name string (the one set at construction); the mutant returns a fixed literal "MUTATED_NAME" so it violates this by returning a different string for some inputs.

For every input string s, calling name() on the reference token returns the same stored token name (the constructor-set name), whereas the mutant returns a fixed literal "MUTATED_NAME" that differs from the stored name for some inputs — so there exists an input (the stored name) for which the mutant's return differs from the reference.

For any fuzzed address caller, calling name() on the correct contract returns the constructor-set token name (stored in the contract), whereas the mutant returns a fixed literal "MUTATED_NAME" which differs from the stored name for some deployed-name choices; the test asserts that name() equals the expected constructor name (so the reference always satisfies it and the mutant fails for at least some inputs).

For any deployed C, its name() view returns the constructor-initialized token name string (the stored _name); the mutant always returns the literal "MUTATED_NAME" and thus differs for at least those deployments where the constructor name is not "MUTATED_NAME".

For any fuzzed arbitrary string used as the token name at deployment time, the reference C preserves and returns that constructor-set name via name(), while the mutant always returns the fixed literal "MUTATED_NAME" and therefore will differ for some deployed names.

For every input address caller, the reference contract's symbol() returns the stored ERC20 symbol string (not a fixed literal); the mutant returns the constant "DCT" breaking this when the stored symbol differs (e.g., any caller observing symbol() will sometimes see a value not equal to the stored _symbol), so calling symbol() and comparing to the known stored name distinguishes them.
